title: SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I, 1943)
summary: A reviewing court must assess an agency’s action on the grounds the agency actually invoked and cannot supply a discretionary rationale the agency never adopted.
notes: Frankfurter's opinion supplies the rule that 'an administrative order cannot be upheld unless the grounds upon which the agency acted in exercising its powers were those upon which its action can be sustained'; the company was Federal Water Service Corporation.

sections.Parties: The SEC defended its approval of a reorganization plan for Federal Water Service Corporation. The respondents were officers, directors, and controlling shareholders whose preferred shares received different treatment from those held by outside investors.
sections.Material Facts: While negotiating reorganization plans, management purchased 12,407 preferred shares in the market to protect its position in the reorganized company. Equal treatment of those shares would have given management more than ten percent of the new common stock. The SEC found no fraud, concealment, inside-information advantage, unfair price, or harm from the particular purchases. It nevertheless treated management as fiduciaries barred by established equitable principles from receiving the same conversion benefit as other preferred shareholders. The approved plan required management’s shares to be surrendered for cost plus interest.
sections.Procedural History: The managers petitioned for review and the court of appeals affirmed the SEC's order, 128 F.2d 303 (D.C. Cir. 1942). The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed, holding that the order could not stand on the grounds the Commission had stated. Frankfurter wrote; Black dissented joined by Reed and Murphy; Douglas took no part.
sections.Issue: Could the order be sustained on judicial fiduciary rules that did not prohibit the transactions, or on the Commission’s statutory expertise and policy judgment offered in court but not actually used in the original decision?
sections.Holding: The SEC’s order could not be upheld on the legal ground it invoked. A reviewing court could not affirm by making the policy determination Congress entrusted to the Commission when the Commission had not made that determination. The result did not deny the SEC authority to adopt a lawful standard on an adequate basis.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority examined what the agency actually said, rather than treating the word fiduciary as an answer to every question about duty and remedy. Established equitable doctrine did not forbid corporate managers from buying stock merely because of their positions. Since the SEC disavowed fraud or misuse of the particular circumstances and relied on existing judicial rules, those rules could not sustain its order.

The statutory public-interest and fair-and-equitable standards gave the Commission substantial authority to develop protections informed by experience. But recognizing that possible authority did not supply an exercise of it. Courts may affirm a lower court on another legal ground within their own authority; they cannot substitute their own discretionary administrative judgment for the agency’s. Clear disclosure and adequate support of the agency’s actual grounds make review possible and respect the allocation of responsibility. The dissent disputed the majority’s reading of the agency’s reasons rather than simply rejecting the need for reasons.
